title: Chapter 11: Exceptions, Validation, and Failure Design
description: Treat failures as API behavior rather than afterthoughts. Learners choose checked or unchecked semantics from caller recovery, translate infrastructure errors without losing causes, read cause and suppressed chains, establish resource ownership with try-with-resources, and design validation and user messages that aid correction without exposing sensitive internals.

lessons.title: Throwable hierarchy and checked versus unchecked exceptions
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Throwable hierarchy and checked versus unchecked exceptions

## Failure categories
Throwable is the root. Error generally represents conditions ordinary application code should not attempt to recover from. Exception includes checked exceptions and RuntimeException subclasses. Checked exceptions must be caught or declared; unchecked does not mean harmless.
```java
static String load(java.nio.file.Path path) throws java.io.IOException {
    return java.nio.file.Files.readString(path);
}
```
The signature tells callers that file access can fail. A caller able to choose another file may recover; a service boundary may translate the failure into an application-level response. IllegalArgumentException commonly indicates a violated input contract.

## Design decision
Checked exceptions can make expected recovery obligations visible, but blindly wrapping every failure into RuntimeException discards that benefit. Conversely, forcing catches for programming defects often leads to meaningless handlers. Select a policy based on the caller's useful response and the abstraction boundary.

## Practice
Classify file missing, invalid domain amount, index bug, exhausted heap, and interrupted wait. Write the recovery action or explain why recovery belongs elsewhere. Never catch Throwable just to continue; it can hide serious runtime conditions and cancellation.

lessons.title: try-with-resources, ownership, and suppressed exceptions
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# try-with-resources, ownership, and suppressed exceptions

## Own the lifetime
```java
try (var reader = java.nio.file.Files.newBufferedReader(path);
     var writer = java.nio.file.Files.newBufferedWriter(output)) {
    writer.write(reader.readLine());
}
```
Resources implementing AutoCloseable close when the block exits normally or exceptionally, in reverse declaration order. If opening the second resource fails, the first still closes. If the body fails and close also fails, the body exception remains primary and close failures are suppressed.

## Ownership is separate from usage
A method that opens a stream usually owns closure. A method receiving a caller-owned stream should document whether it closes it; surprising closure can break later work. Closing a buffered wrapper normally closes its underlying stream. Files.lines returns a resource-backed stream and also requires closure.

Resource cleanup is different from garbage collection. A socket or file descriptor can exhaust an operating-system limit long before heap pressure triggers collection.

## Practice
Create a small AutoCloseable whose close records its name; nest two and verify reverse order. Make both the body and close throw, then inspect getSuppressed(). Write a copy function with an explicit ownership policy. Handle an empty file before passing null from readLine to writer.write.

exercises.title: try-with-resources, ownership, and suppressed exceptions: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: If both the body and close fail in try-with-resources, which failure is primary?
choices: The close failure always replaces the body
The body's failure, with close failure suppressed
hints: try-with-resources keeps the body's failure as primary and attaches any exception thrown by close() as a suppressed exception, retrievable via getSuppressed().

lessons.title: Chapter 11 assessment and deliberate practice
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Chapter 11 assessment

Before touching the debugger, use this chapter's rules on cause preservation and exception translation to predict what **Preserve the original cause** should print, then run it and repair the defect so the caught NumberFormatException survives as the thrown exception's cause.

The parsePort function lab exercises boundary validation in isolation; it is not proof of every competency from checked-versus-unchecked design through safe user-facing error reporting covered across the chapter's five lessons. Review the repaired source and explain why forwarding the cause matters for diagnosis, without consulting the answer.

The specific exception type that caused the outage

exercises.title: Chapter 11 implementation lab: parsePort
exercises.instructionMarkdown:
Implement `parsePort`. Parse a decimal port from 1 through 65535; return -1 for malformed or out-of-range text. Write the precondition and boundary table first, keep the method deterministic, and do not print.

Use Integer.parseInt spelling rules with no whitespace trimming, then require 1..65535. Malformed and out-of-range values return -1.
hints: Decide separately whether the text is a syntactically valid decimal integer (Integer.parseInt, no trimming) and whether the parsed value falls within 1..65535.
Check the boundaries 0, 1, 65535, and 65536, plus malformed and whitespace-padded text, before submitting.

exercises.title: Preserve the original cause
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Repair the exception translation so the caught NumberFormatException is passed as the cause of the thrown IllegalArgumentException, and the program writes exactly `true`. Keep the two-exception structure and explain why forwarding the cause makes the getCause() check pass, rather than hard-coding the print statement. Output tests verify the printed result; confirming the cause is genuinely preserved requires reading the source.
hints: Pass the caught exception as the translated exception's cause.
